spoken: From November 1942 to May 1943, the Second World War was fought across Tunisia.
An American reporter wrote about it in a tent. A British tank officer turned it into poems.
In occupied Tunis, a Jewish lawyer kept a diary. A young man from the city's Jewish quarter later made it a novel.
Four writers, four places to stand. This is the war in Tunisia, in words.
In 1942, Tunisia was a French protectorate, ruled in name by the Bey of Tunis.
On the 8th of November, the Allies landed in Morocco and Algeria. The next day, German aircraft landed at Tunis.
German and Italian troops held Tunis, Bizerte and the east, as Allied armies closed in from Algeria and Libya.
Tunisians of every faith, Muslims, Jews and Christians, lived through the occupation and the fighting.
On the 7th of May 1943, Allied troops entered Tunis and Bizerte. On the 13th of May, the last Axis armies in Africa surrendered.
Our four writers each saw a different part of those six months.
Ernie Pyle followed American soldiers on the western front, from the central plains to the northern hills.
Keith Douglas fought with British tanks from Egypt across Libya, and reached Tunisia in the spring.
Paul Ghez lived the occupation inside Tunis, as one of the leaders of its Jewish community.
And Albert Memmi, a young man from Tunis's Jewish quarter, saw it from the city, then from a labour camp.
Two of their books came out in 1943, while the war went on. One came out in 1946, and one in 1953.
For each, we'll ask who wrote it, what kind of book it is, and what is fact or fiction.
Ernie Pyle, a Scripps-Howard newspaper columnist, came to North Africa in late 1942, and lived as the American soldiers did.
In February 1943, he retreated with them from Sbaytla. In March, he was at Gafsa, retaken in the south.
In April, he joined the First Infantry Division in the hills before Mateur, and in May, he reached Bizerte.
This is reportage, made of short columns written within days, and collected in 1943 as a book, Here Is Your War.
His column ran in 42 newspapers in November 1942, and in 122 by April 1943.
He left the generals' view to others. In his own words, I only know what we see from our worm's-eye view.
That view was tired men, mud, fear and graves, with the soldiers named, and their home towns, often their streets.
It is reporting, not fiction. But it shows only what one American saw, and what the army's censors let through.
Tunisians stay at its edges, often seen through French officers' prejudices, though he noted that both armies cleared Arab families from the fighting.
He won the Pulitzer Prize in 1944, and was killed in the Pacific in April 1945.
Keith Douglas was a British poet and, at 22, a tank officer in the Egyptian desert.
At El Allamain in October 1942, he left a staff job and went to his regiment without orders.
With the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry he fought across Libya, until a mine wounded him at Wadi Zem Zem in January 1943.
In hospital he began the war poems that made his name, then that spring rejoined his regiment, now in Tunisia.
His prose book, Allamain to Zem Zem, is a memoir of his months in the desert, up to the day he was wounded.
He illustrated it with his own drawings. It came out in 1946, two years after his death.
A memoir tells real events, as its writer remembers and chooses them. His colonel, Edward Kellett, appears under a nickname.
His poems go further. In a poem whose German title means forget me not, soldiers return to a battlefield three weeks after a fight.
They find the German gunner who had hit the narrator's tank, and a photograph signed by his girlfriend, Steffi.
Douglas wrote, For here the lover and killer are mingled. The poem sees both in one man.
He went back to England in December 1943, and was killed in Normandy on the 9th of June 1944, aged 24.
Paul Ghez, born in Soos in 1898, was a lawyer in Tunis and a member of its Jewish community council.
With the German troops came an SS unit under Walter Rowf. Tunisia's Jews faced fines, confiscations, hostage-taking and forced labour.
In December, the SS demanded Jewish workers. The community's leaders had to form a committee to recruit them, headed by Ghez.
His book is a diary, in dated entries, from November 1942 to May 1943.
He called it, in French, Six Months under the Boot. It was printed in Tunis in 1943.
It records the orders and the lists. By the 14th of December, he counts 3,585 men recruited.
Some marched to a camp at Shaylus. Others worked at airfields, or near the front.
Families came to his office to ask for their sons, and he tried to bring the numbers down.
In all, about 5,000 Jewish men were forced to work, in some forty camps, by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's estimate.
On the 7th of May, as the Allies entered Tunis, he arranged the workers' return. The next day, he found his flat emptied.
Nothing in it is invented. But it is one man's view, from a terrible position between German orders and the families.
Other accounts of those months exist, and the historian Hayim Sadoon notes that they do not always agree.
Albert Memmi was born in 1920 by the Hara, the old Jewish quarter of Tunis, a saddler's son.
At home he spoke the Arabic of Tunis's Jews. A scholarship took him to the French lee-say.
In 1942 and 1943, he went to a forced labour camp, more or less of his own free will, as he later said.
In 1953, he published his first novel, The Pillar of Salt, with a preface by Albert Camus.
It is a novel. Its narrator has another name, Alexandre Mordekai Benilloosh.
Alexandre grows up in an alley by the Hara, goes to the French lee-say, and feels a stranger in his own city.
Vichy France's anti-Jewish laws tell him he will never be fully French.
When the Germans demand Jewish workers, Memmi has him say, I asked to go, because it was intolerable to stay.
In the camp, Alexandre keeps a diary, and later escapes with friends.
Much of this is Memmi's own life. The historian Hayim Sadoon argues that the novel rests on his camp diary.
The ending is invented. Alexandre sails for South America, while Memmi studied in Algiers and Paris, taught in Tunis, then settled in France.
The title recalls Lot's wife in Genesis, turned to salt for looking back. A novel looks back too.
Lay the four books side by side, across the same six months.
Pyle saw the front from the American side. Douglas saw the desert war from a British tank.
Ghez saw what soldiers never saw, the occupation, from inside the Jewish community of Tunis.
Memmi lived it as a young Tunisian Jew, and ten years later reshaped it as fiction.
Reportage is fast and close, but censored. A diary is exact about dates, but sees from one desk.
A memoir chooses what to remember. A novel invents, to show what a life felt like.
Four men's books still tell little of the Muslim families whose fields became battlefields, the women of Tunis, or Italian and German soldiers.
No single book is the whole war. Read together, and with care, they show far more of it.
Ask of every book who wrote it, from where, and when, and the war in Tunisia comes closer.
